summary: This unit teaches you to lead a small electrical crew as a leading hand, in support of your supervisor. You will learn to set the example on safety, quality and honesty, communicate clearly, plan and delegate work, give feedback and develop people, build trust, handle conflict and problems, make sound decisions within your authority, and lead change while protecting the company's name.

blocks.p: At Level 3 you are no longer only responsible for your own work. As a **leading hand** (crew leader, chargehand) you run a small crew on site, day to day, for a supervisor or manager who may visit only now and then. You do not hire, fire or set prices, but the crew's safety, the quality of its work and the client's opinion of the company depend a great deal on you. This unit is about doing that well.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Set the example
Follow safe isolation, wear PPE, keep time, do neat work and tell the truth, every day, so the crew copies the right things.
Lead on safety
Stop unsafe work at once, deal with the cause, and make it easy for the crew to raise concerns.
Act ethically
Refuse gifts and deals that compromise you, declare conflicts of interest, and never falsify records or skip tests.
Communicate
Run toolbox talks, give clear instructions and check they were understood, listen actively, and report to the supervisor.
Plan and delegate
Share out tasks by skill and development, set clear goals, delegate with a proper brief and follow-up, and stay accountable.
Develop people
Give positive and corrective feedback, recognise good work, coach and mentor apprentices, and induct new workers.
Build trust and respect
Keep promises, be fair, keep private matters private, stop disrespect and harassment, and look after wellbeing.
Handle problems and conflict
Make informed decisions, solve problems at their cause, settle disputes fairly, and pass on what is outside your authority.
Lead change and protect the company's image
Explain and introduce new rules and methods, behave well on clients' premises, and learn from each job.

blocks.p: **Management** is planning, organising and controlling the work: the jobs, the materials, the schedule. **Leadership** is getting people to want to do the work well: by example, by clear direction, by fairness and by caring about them. A leading hand needs both, but on a small crew it is your leadership the crew notices most.

blocks.note: Jamaican crews often mix long-serving tradesmen, young electricians and apprentices from HEART/NSTA Trust programmes. Respect for experience matters, and so does giving young workers a chance to grow. A good leading hand uses both: the experience of the older hands and the energy and new skills of the younger ones.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: The leading hand's role and authority

blocks.p: You are the link between the crew and the supervisor. You turn the supervisor's plan into the day's work, and you carry the crew's problems, ideas and progress back up.

head: Usually within a leading hand's authority
Usually needs the supervisor or manager
rows: The order of the day's tasks
Who does which task in the crew
Stopping unsafe work
Small changes in method that do not change the design
Asking for materials, tools and help
Correcting a crew member on the spot
Changes to the design or the drawings
Extra work not in the contract, and its price
Overtime and its cost
Hiring, discipline beyond a first word, dismissal
Promises to the client about dates or money
Changing company policy

blocks.p: When something is outside your authority, do not ignore it and do not decide it anyway. Note it, tell the person asking that the supervisor will confirm, and pass it on promptly, in writing if possible. If the drawings clash with the building (an outlet shown where a door now stands), hold that part of the work and ask; do not guess.

ul: Carry out the agreed plan, and tell the supervisor **early** when something will stop it: a late delivery, a missing drawing, a sick worker.
Bring options, not only problems: 'The wall is not ready; we can do the board this morning instead.'
Give a short daily report: work done, problems found, materials needed, plans for tomorrow.
Back the supervisor's decisions in front of the crew. If you disagree, say so to the supervisor in private.
Never promise what you cannot deliver. If a deadline cannot be met safely, say so with the reasons.

blocks.h: Supporting leadership when you are not the leader

blocks.p: An experienced electrician who is not the leading hand supports leadership by backing the leader's plan, offering ideas and warnings to the leader (not giving the crew different orders), helping newer workers, and setting a good example. Undermining the leader in front of the crew damages everyone's work.

The company's **policies and procedures** set its rules on safety, behaviour, vehicles, phones and social media, gifts, private work, leave, harassment and discipline. A leading hand must know them, follow them and apply them fairly. When in doubt, check the policy or ask the supervisor.

sections.title: Leading by example: safety, standards and ethics

blocks.p: The crew copies what you **do**, not what you **say**. If you skip lock-off 'just for a minute', walk on site without boots, or leave a board untidy, the crew learns that the rules are optional.

head: Example you set
What the crew learns
rows: Safe isolation every time: off, lock, tag, prove dead with a tester proved before and after
Safe isolation is not negotiable, even for small jobs.
Full PPE, even for a quick look
Rules apply to everyone, including the leader.
Arriving on time; starting the toolbox talk on time; keeping promises
Time and people's word matter.
Neat work checked against the drawing and specification
What 'good' looks like on this job.
Owning your mistakes
It is safe to admit errors, so problems are found early.
Speaking politely to clients, other trades and the crew
Respect is how this company works.

ul: **Stop unsafe work at once.** If someone is about to work on a circuit that is not locked off, or use a damaged ladder, stop the work first and talk second.
Then find out why it happened: time pressure, missing equipment (not enough padlocks or testers), or not knowing the procedure. Fix that cause.
Report as the company's procedure requires, and remind the whole crew at the next toolbox talk without naming and shaming anyone.
Take damaged tools, leads and ladders out of use: tag them and report them.
Make it easy to raise concerns. A crew member who says 'I am not trained on that' is helping you, not slowing you down.
Never let anyone who seems impaired (by alcohol, ganja, medication or exhaustion) do electrical work, work at height or drive.

blocks.note: A worker who is unsteady, smells strongly of alcohol or seems 'out of it' must be taken off electrical and height work at once, kept safe, not allowed to drive, and reported to the supervisor as the company's policy says. Whatever the law on carrying small amounts of ganja, being impaired at work is a safety matter. Deal with it privately and respectfully.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: **Integrity** means being honest and doing the right thing even when nobody is watching. A company's **code of conduct** sets out how staff must behave. As leading hand, you face ethical pressure more often than the crew.

head: Situation
The right response
rows: A supplier offers you a gift if you order from them
Refuse it politely and tell your manager. A gift that could sway a decision is a bribe, whatever it is called.
A relative or friend owns a business the company could buy from

This is a **conflict of interest**: your private interest could affect a decision you make for your employer. Declare it to your supervisor and let the company decide through its normal buying process.
A client offers you private work, for cash, outside the company
Follow the company's policy on private work. Taking the company's clients for yourself competes with your employer; refer the request to the company.
A client or colleague asks you to skip a test, or to sign for work not done
Refuse and explain why: the tests prove the installation is safe, and a false record is dishonest and may be illegal.
A crew member asks you to sign him in for time he was not there
Refuse. Timesheets are records the company pays from. Record the real times.
A crew member posts photos of a client's premises, alarm panel or layout online
Ask for them to be removed at once, explain the security and confidentiality risk, and report it as the policy says.

blocks.p: A **toolbox talk** (pre-start briefing) is a short meeting, usually 5 to 15 minutes, at the start of a shift or a new task. Its purpose is to brief the crew on the day's tasks, who does what, the hazards and their controls, and what to do in an emergency.

flow: Prepare: read the job plan, drawings and risk assessment; list the tasks and who does each
Note the hazards specific to today and the controls for each
Add the emergency points: first-aider, first-aid kit, exits, assembly point, nearest hospital, who to call
Hold it at the work area, where everyone can see and hear
Speak plainly; show equipment; keep to a few key points
Check understanding with questions
Invite concerns and deal with them
Everyone signs the attendance sheet; keep it with the job file

ul: Say **what** is to be done, **why**, to what **standard**, **by when**, and with which drawing, tools and materials.
One task at a time for a new worker; the whole job for an experienced one.
**Check understanding**: ask the person to explain back, in their own words, the key steps or how they will isolate. 'Any questions?' is not enough: people rarely say they did not understand.
On a noisy site, move somewhere quiet, or show rather than tell.

blocks.p: **Active listening** means giving the speaker your full attention: look at them, put your phone away, let them finish, ask questions, and repeat back the main point ('So the problem is the chase is too shallow for the box?'). Crew members who are listened to raise problems early.

Crews often talk in Patois among themselves, and that is fine. With clients, visiting engineers and inspectors, speak clear standard English and avoid trade slang they may not know. With apprentices, explain trade words the first time. Match your words to your listener.

head: Barrier
What helps
rows: Noise, distance, phone signal
Talk face to face in a quiet spot; confirm by text or in writing.
Jargon or unclear words
Plain words; show on the drawing or the actual equipment.
Assumptions ('they know that')
Check understanding every time it matters.
Strong feelings: anger, embarrassment
Wait until people are calm; talk in private.
Reading and writing difficulties
Explain out loud and demonstrate; never embarrass the person.

blocks.p: A good site meeting has a clear purpose, a few points, and ends with agreed actions: who does what by when. Hold it where people can hear, include everyone affected (including the newest workers), keep to time and write the actions down.

Your daily or weekly report to the supervisor gives: work done against the plan, problems found and what you did, materials and help needed, safety matters and incidents, and tomorrow's plan. Report bad news as well as good: a supervisor who hears about a problem early can usually fix it.
Goals give the crew a clear target. Use **SMART** goals:

head: Letter
Meaning
Example
rows: S
Specific: exactly what
Fix and wire the 24 outlet boxes in Block B
M
Measurable: you can count or check it
All 24, checked against the drawing
A
Achievable with the people, time and materials you have
Two electricians, materials on site
R
Relevant to the job's plan
Needed before the plasterers start on Monday
T
Time-bound: by when
By Friday at 3 p.m.

ul: Match tasks to each person's skill, and give each person something that stretches them a little.
Share the dirty and dull jobs fairly; do not always give them to the newest person.
Rotate tasks so people learn, but not on a day when there is no time to supervise.
Show the plan visibly: a simple chart or a **Gantt chart** (tasks as bars along a time scale) helps everyone see who does what and when.

blocks.p: **Delegation** is giving a task, and the authority to do it, to someone else, while you stay **accountable** for the result. The person doing it is responsible for doing it properly; you are still answerable to the supervisor.

flow: Choose a task you are allowed to hand over and that the person can do, or can learn safely with help
Brief them: what, why, the standard, the drawing or specification, the hazards and controls, the tools and materials, and the deadline
Show them the first one if it is new to them
Ask them to explain back the main steps
Agree when you will check, and how to get help
Let them work; do not hover or take over
Check at the agreed points, early enough to catch mistakes
Inspect at the end, give feedback and record it

blocks.p: Some tasks are not delegated to a junior worker: signing test certificates, deciding protective device ratings, agreeing prices or extra work with the client, and any live testing they are not authorised for.

blocks.h: Matching your style to the person

head: The person
Style that suits
What you do
rows: New to the task, keen but unskilled
**Directing**
Clear step-by-step instructions, show them, check closely.
Some skill, still building confidence
**Coaching**
Explain why, ask questions that lead them to the answer, praise progress.
Skilled but unsure or unmotivated
**Supporting**
Listen, encourage, involve them in decisions.
Skilled and confident
**Delegating**
Give the whole task and the outcome; check at milestones.

blocks.p: Style also depends on the situation. In an emergency (a fire, a shock, an arc flash) there is no time to consult: the leader gives short, direct orders. When planning next week's work, asking the crew's views gives better plans and more commitment.

sections.title: Developing people: feedback, recognition, coaching and induction

head: Point
Positive feedback
Corrective feedback
rows: Purpose
Tells the person what they did well, so they keep doing it
Tells the person what must change, and how
Where
Can be given in front of the crew
In private
How
Specific: say exactly what was good and why it matters
Describe what you saw and its effect; ask their view; agree the fix; offer help
Example
'Kimarley, your labels on DB-2 match the chart exactly; that will save time at testing.'
'Two of the glands were only hand-tight. Water will get in and trip the GFCI. Let's tighten these and I will check the next two with you.'

ul: Give feedback **soon**, about the **work**, not the person. 'This joint is loose' helps; 'You are careless' does not.
Give much more positive than corrective feedback. People trust criticism from a leader who also notices good work.
Never give feedback in anger. Wait until you are calm.
Follow up: check that the change has been made, and say so when it has.

blocks.p: Recognise good work by thanking the person by name, saying exactly what they did, telling the supervisor, and giving them a chance at more responsible work. Recognition costs nothing, and crews that feel noticed work harder and stay longer. Never promise rewards (a bonus, a raise) you have no power to give.

**Coaching** helps someone improve a particular skill, often by asking questions that lead them to the answer ('What does the drawing say? What would happen if water got in?') rather than doing it for them. **Mentoring** is a longer relationship in which an experienced worker (the **mentor**) guides and advises a less experienced one about the trade and their career.

flow: Explain: what and why
Show: do it once, slowly, talking through it
Let them try, while you watch
Check and give feedback
Let them practise until it is right every time

blocks.p: On a new worker's first day, make sure they get a **site induction**: the hazards, the site rules, safe isolation as this company does it, exits and assembly point, first aid, who is who and who to ask. Pair them with a reliable worker for the first days, and check on them often. Do not send a new worker to work alone on day one.

ul: Explain **why** the work and deadlines matter, not only what to do.
Thank people for extra effort, specifically.
Give people some say in how they do their work.
Be fair: fairness in overtime, tasks and treatment matters more to most crews than speeches.
Keep promises; do not use threats ('you can be replaced').

head: Trust builder
What it looks like
rows: Keep your word
If you said you would ask about overtime, you ask, and report back, even when the answer is no.
Be fair and consistent
The same rules for everyone; no favourites; overtime offered in turn from an open list.
Be honest
Tell the crew the truth about problems; admit your mistakes and fix them.
Keep confidences
Health, money and family matters told to you in private stay private.
Back the crew
Listen to their concerns, give credit to the person who did the good work, and never push them to cut safety corners.

blocks.p: Trust is slow to build and quick to lose. If you give the crew wrong information (the wrong cable size, the wrong drawing), stop the work, admit it, and plan the correction. Blaming the stores clerk or hiding the mistake costs far more trust than the mistake itself.

Sometimes you agree a special arrangement for one person, such as different hours while a family member is ill. Others may complain of favouritism. Explain that arrangements are made fairly, according to need and company policy, and that anyone in a similar situation would be treated the same way, **without sharing the person's private details**.

ul: Everyone on the crew is treated with respect, whatever their sex, age, religion, background, disability or where they come from.
Jokes, nicknames or comments that demean someone, and any unwanted sexual comments or contact, are stopped at once. Make it clear that everyone gets respect.
Do not move or isolate the person who is being targeted; deal with those doing it.
Report harassment as the company's policy says. Jamaican law requires employers to deal with sexual harassment, and most companies have a written policy.

blocks.p: Watch for changes: a cheerful worker who goes quiet, makes unusual mistakes, is often late or seems exhausted. Ask privately and kindly whether they are all right, and listen. You are not a counsellor, but you can adjust work for the day, keep them off high-risk tasks if they are not fit, and point them to help the company offers. Long night shifts and heat also cause fatigue: plan breaks, water and rotation of tiring tasks.

head: Stage
What you see
What the leader does
rows: Forming
A new crew is polite and unsure of roles
Give clear roles, rules and goals.
Storming
Arguments over roles, methods and status
Listen, clarify roles, set ground rules, deal with conflict fairly.
Norming
The crew agrees ways of working
Involve them more; recognise progress.
Performing
The crew works well with little direction
Delegate more; develop individuals.

flow: Be clear what must be decided, and by when
Gather the facts: drawings, distances, costs, hazards, the client's needs, what the contract says
Ask the crew's views: they often know practical problems you have missed
List the options with their good and bad points for safety, quality, cost, time and the client
Put safety first
Check your authority; take what is beyond it to the supervisor
Decide, explain the decision and record it
Check later whether it worked

blocks.p: Fixing the same problem every day wastes time. If the crew keeps running out of fixings mid-shift, sending someone to the hardware store each time treats the symptom. Working out how many are used and keeping a minimum stock on the van removes the cause.

flow: Stop the argument in front of others, and make sure the work is left safe
Talk to the people involved in private, one side at a time if needed
Let each person explain without interruption; listen actively
Keep to the work and the facts, not personalities
Look for an answer both can accept; often each side has a good point
Decide if it is yours to decide, explain why, and record the outcome
Pass it to the supervisor if it is beyond your authority or keeps happening
Check later that the bad feeling has gone

blocks.p: **Conflict with another trade** (the plumbers keep cutting your chases or moving your materials) is handled leader to leader: talk privately with their leading hand, agree the sequence of work and where materials are kept, using the programme and drawings, and involve the site supervisor or main contractor if it cannot be settled. Tell your own crew not to argue with the other trade on site.

When someone's timekeeping or work slips, speak to them privately first, find out why, and agree a plan with a date to review it. Record what was agreed. If it continues, it goes to the supervisor under the company's procedures. Shaming someone in front of the crew, or ignoring the problem because 'his work is good', both make things worse.

When a client is angry, stay calm, listen without interrupting, acknowledge the problem, explain the facts without blaming others, say what you will do and by when, and do it. If something your crew caused (dust on furniture, a scratched wall), apologise and put it right at once. Never shout back, and never walk away and leave the crew to deal with it.

sections.title: Leading change, the company's image and growing as a leader

flow: Understand the change yourself; ask the supervisor about anything unclear
Work out what it means for your crew and your job; get any new equipment in place
Explain what is changing, why, and what each person must do
Show how: demonstrate the new method, app or equipment
Let the crew ask questions and raise concerns; take real problems back to the supervisor
Follow the new way yourself, every time
Check, correct politely but firmly, and praise those who follow it

blocks.p: People resist change for real reasons: fear of looking slow, more paperwork, or a genuine flaw in the new method. Listen; their concern may improve the change. Do not let people keep the old way 'because they prefer it', and do not do their part for them.
On a client's premises, your crew **is** the company. Clients judge the whole company by what they see and hear.

ul: Arrive on time, in clean work clothes with company ID if issued; greet the client politely.
Explain the day's work, which rooms you need and when the power will be off.
Protect the premises: dust sheets, floor mats, vacuum drill dust, tidy as you go.
No loud music, smoking, bad language or using the client's things without asking.
Keep the client's information, layouts and security arrangements private; no photos on social media.
At the end, show the client the work, explain switches and labels, and leave the place clean.

blocks.p: After a job, hold a short **debrief** (job review) with the crew: what went well, what went badly, what to do differently next time. Keep it blame-free, write down the lessons and pass the useful ones to the supervisor.

ul: Ask your supervisor and crew for feedback on your leadership.
Learn from a mentor you respect.
Take short courses in supervision, safety and communication; HEART/NSTA Trust and other training bodies offer them.
Reflect on difficult days: what would you do differently?

blocks.p: Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can explain the leading hand's role and say which decisions are within my authority and which go to the supervisor.
I can support the supervisor with early warnings, options and clear reports.
I can set an example on safety, quality, time-keeping and honesty, and explain why it matters.
I can stop unsafe work, deal with its cause and handle a worker who seems impaired.
I can respond correctly to gifts, conflicts of interest, private-work offers and requests to falsify records.
I can plan and deliver a toolbox talk and check that it was understood.
I can give clear instructions, listen actively and adapt how I speak to my listener.
I can write SMART goals and share out work fairly.
I can delegate a task with a proper brief and follow-up, and explain who is accountable.
I can choose a leadership style to suit the person and the situation.
I can give positive and corrective feedback, recognise good work, coach and mentor.
I can induct a new worker safely.
I can build trust, keep confidences while being fair, and stop disrespect and harassment.
I can notice and respond to wellbeing problems.
I can make an informed decision, solve problems at their cause and handle conflict within the crew and with other trades.
I can lead a change and protect the company's image on a client's premises.

terms: Accountable
Answerable for a result, even when someone else did the work.
Active listening
Giving full attention, asking questions and repeating back the main points.
Code of conduct
The written rules on how staff are expected to behave at work.
Coaching
Helping someone improve a skill, often by asking questions that lead them to the answer.
Concession of authority (limits of authority)
The boundary of the decisions a leading hand may make; beyond it, the supervisor decides.
Conflict of interest
When a worker's private interests could affect a decision they make for their employer.
Corrective feedback
Feedback, given privately, on what must change and how.
Debrief
A short meeting after a job to review what went well and what to improve.
Delegation
Giving a task and the authority to do it to someone else, while staying accountable.
Gantt chart
A chart showing tasks as bars along a time scale.
Induction
Introducing a new worker to the site's hazards, rules, people and their role.
Integrity
Being honest and keeping to strong moral principles, even when nobody is watching.
Leading hand
The worker who leads a small crew day to day for a supervisor.
Mentor
An experienced worker who guides a less experienced one over a long period.
Positive feedback
Specific praise of good work, to encourage more of it.
SMART
Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound: a way to write clear goals.
Toolbox talk
A short briefing at the start of a shift on the tasks, hazards and controls.

c1.title: A new leading hand at a Rose Hall villa
c1.text: Dwight Morrison has just been made leading hand of a four-person crew wiring a large villa at Rose Hall, St James. Errol Pusey, who has 20 years in the trade and was leading hand on the last job, is now in Dwight's crew. Shanoy, a first-year apprentice, has just joined. The supervisor, Mrs Barrett, visits twice a week and has asked for all second fix to be finished by Thursday, but the drywall contractor is two days behind.

c2.title: Night shifts at a Constant Spring supermarket
c2.text: Kadian Walters leads a crew of five on night shifts refitting the lighting of a supermarket in Constant Spring, St Andrew. The store closes at 10 p.m. and the crew starts at 10:30 p.m. The work uses a scissor lift and means shutting down one sub-board at a time, while cleaners and a forklift restocking shelves work nearby. Two of the crew are new to the company.

c3.title: Pathway lights at an Oracabessa hotel
c3.text: At a small hotel in Oracabessa, St Mary, leading hand Sasha-Gaye Thompson must hand the fitting of 30 outdoor pathway lights to Rushane, a third-year apprentice, while she rewires the main board. Rushane has fitted indoor lights before but never outdoor fittings, which need cable glands tightened to the maker's torque so that water cannot get in.

c4.title: Friction at an Alexandria health centre
c4.text: Omari Hylton leads an electrical crew at a new health centre in Alexandria, St Ann. The plumbing crew keeps cutting across the electricians' chases and moving their materials, and yesterday members of the two crews shouted at each other. Omari's crew is new and still arguing about who does which task. Separately, Nickeisha has told Omari in private that her mother is in hospital, and Omari has agreed she can start an hour later this week.

c5.title: Pressures on a Seaforth school job
c5.text: Kevaughn Brissett leads a crew rewiring a primary school in Seaforth, St Thomas. His cousin owns a hardware store that could supply the job's fittings. The school's principal privately asks Kevaughn to wire her house 'for cash, outside your company'. One crew member asks Kevaughn to sign him in for a morning he missed, and another has posted photos of the school's new alarm panel on social media.

questions.q: Errol keeps contradicting Dwight's instructions in front of the crew. What is Dwight's best first step?
o: Talk to Errol privately, ask for his support and agree how to disagree
Correct Errol firmly in front of the crew, so they see who is in charge
Ask Mrs Barrett to move Errol to another crew before the job slips
Let Errol give the instructions, since he has far more experience
questions.why: Disagreement in front of the crew confuses everyone and undermines the plan. A private talk that respects Errol's experience, asks for his support and agrees that disagreements come to Dwight first usually solves it. If it continues, it goes to the supervisor.

questions.q: Dwight gives Errol a whole task with few details, but gives Shanoy step-by-step instructions and checks him often. Is this right?
o: No: every worker must get exactly the same instructions to be fair
No: Shanoy will never learn unless he is left alone to work it out
Yes, but only because Errol was the leading hand on the last job
Yes: the style suits each person's skill and experience
questions.why: Good leaders match their style to the person: directing a new, unskilled worker closely, and delegating whole tasks to a skilled, confident one. Fairness means fair treatment, not identical instructions. Errol's past role has nothing to do with it.

questions.q: With the drywall two days late, the crew say Thursday is impossible. What should Dwight do?
o: Promise Thursday anyway, and ask the crew to work faster to make it
Tell Mrs Barrett now, with what can be done and a new date
Say nothing, since the delay is the drywall contractor's fault
Start fitting accessories before the walls are ready, to save time
questions.why: A supervisor needs bad news early, with options, so the programme can be changed or help arranged. Promising what cannot be done, hiding the problem, or working ahead of the walls (which would have to be redone) all make things worse.

questions.q: Which content is most important in tonight's toolbox talk?
o: The store's history and its plans for the new year
The crew's pay rates and the overtime available
The latest company news and the client's sales targets
Tasks, the lift, forklifts, isolation and emergencies
questions.why: A toolbox talk briefs the crew on today's tasks, the specific hazards (scissor lift, forklift traffic, which sub-board is off and how it is isolated) and the emergency arrangements, which matter even more on a night shift when fewer people are around.

questions.q: One of the new workers says he has never used a scissor lift. What should Kadian do?
o: Show him the controls quickly, and let him start on the low shelves
Give him other work and arrange his training before he uses the lift
Ask him to watch the others for an hour, then let him operate it
Tell him that most people learn the lift on the job, so not to worry
questions.why: Nobody operates a scissor lift without proper training and authorisation. Giving him other work keeps him productive and safe; Kadian records the concern and arranges training. Raising it was the right thing for the worker to do, and he should be thanked for it.

questions.q: On the third night, a crew member falls asleep on his break and is unsteady when he wakes. What should Kadian do?
o: Keep him off the lift and live work, and tell the supervisor
Give him a strong coffee and let him carry on with the work on the lift
Send him home in his own car, so that the others are not slowed down
Say nothing tonight, and mention it at the end of the week's last shift
questions.why: Fatigue on night shifts causes falls and mistakes. A worker who is unsteady must not work at height, do electrical work or drive. Kadian keeps him safe, finds out privately what is wrong, and reports as the policy says; he also looks at breaks and rotation for the whole crew.

questions.q: How should Sasha-Gaye brief Rushane on the outdoor lights?
o: Give him the drawing and tell him to finish the 30 lights by tomorrow
Explain the task and standard, show the first one, agree check-ins
Fit most of the lights herself and give him the last few to finish off
Tell him to ask the hotel's handyman whenever he gets stuck on a light
questions.why: A good brief covers what, why, the standard (glands to the maker's torque), the hazards and the deadline; because outdoor fittings are new to him, she shows him the first one and agrees when she will check. Then she lets him work.

questions.q: Rushane asks why the glands must be torqued when hand-tight 'looks fine'. What is the best answer?
o: Because the hotel's manager is paying for the job to be done that way
Because the maker says so, and there is no need to think about why
Because the supervisor will check every one of them and complain
Because loose glands let water in, which trips GFCIs and corrodes
questions.why: Explaining the reason builds understanding and standards that last when nobody is watching. Water getting past a loose gland causes nuisance tripping, corrosion and possible shock. 'Because I said so' teaches nothing.

questions.q: Rushane gets stuck on how to route a cable into a fitting. Sasha-Gaye asks, 'What does the maker's sheet show? Where would water collect?' instead of doing it for him. What is this?
o: Coaching: questions lead him to work out the answer
Avoiding the job: she should do the difficult part herself
Testing him, to decide whether he should finish the job
Delegating: he is now fully responsible for the outcome
questions.why: Coaching uses questions to help the learner think the problem through, so he can solve the next one on his own. She still stays accountable for the result and checks his work at the agreed points.

questions.q: What is Omari's best way to deal with the clash with the plumbing crew?
o: Talk privately with the plumbing leading hand and agree the sequence
Tell his crew to move the plumbers' materials back if they are moved again
Report the plumbers to the client and stop work until they are removed
Ignore it, as the plumbers are not part of his company or his crew
questions.why: Conflict between trades is settled leader to leader, using the programme and drawings to agree the order of work and where materials are kept. If they cannot agree, the site supervisor or main contractor decides. Retaliation or going straight over people's heads makes it worse.

questions.q: Omari's new crew keep arguing about who does which task. Which stage of team development is this, and what helps?
o: Performing: leave them alone to work it out
Norming: they need more tasks to keep busy
Storming: give clear roles and ground rules
Forming: change the whole crew for a new one
questions.why: Arguments over roles and methods are typical of the storming stage. The leader listens, makes roles and ground rules clear, and deals with conflict fairly, which helps the crew move on to agreed ways of working.

questions.q: Another worker complains that Nickeisha gets 'special treatment' with her later start. What should Omari say?
o: Tell him about her mother, so that he understands the reason
Cancel the later start, so nobody can accuse him of favouritism
Tell him to mind his own business and get on with his work
Say it was agreed for a good reason, and he would get the same
questions.why: Omari must be fair and keep confidences. He explains that the arrangement was agreed under the company's policy for a genuine need, and that anyone in a similar situation would be treated the same way, without sharing Nickeisha's private details.

questions.q: Kevaughn's cousin could supply the fittings. What should Kevaughn do?
o: Order from his cousin, as long as the price is the same as elsewhere
Order from his cousin, but in someone else's name to avoid talk
Never mention the cousin's store to anyone at the company
Declare the link to his supervisor and let the company decide
questions.why: This is a conflict of interest: his private interest could affect a decision he makes for his employer. Declaring it and letting the company buy through its normal process protects him and the company, even if the cousin's store ends up being chosen.

questions.q: How should Kevaughn answer the principal's request to wire her house for cash?
o: Accept, since the work would be done in his own time at weekends
Accept, but use the company's leftover materials to keep it cheap
Accept, and tell the crew to keep the arrangement to themselves
Refer her to the company, as the private-work policy requires
questions.why: Taking an employer's client privately competes with the employer and is usually against company policy; using company materials would be theft. He follows the policy and refers the request to the company.

questions.q: A crew member asks Kevaughn to sign him in for the morning he missed. What should Kevaughn do?
o: Sign him in once, but warn him that he will not do it again
Refuse, record the real times, and explain why he cannot do it
Sign him in, but deduct the hours from his pay next month himself
Ask the rest of the crew to vote on whether to sign him in
questions.why: A timesheet is a record the company pays from; signing for time not worked is dishonest. Kevaughn refuses, records the real times, and explains calmly. If the pressure continues, he tells the supervisor. He has no authority to make his own pay deductions.

questions.q: What should Kevaughn do about the photos of the school's alarm panel online?
o: Ask for them to be removed now, explain the risk and report it
Nothing, since the photos show good work the company can be proud of
Post a comment under them, saying that the work is not finished
Wait until the job ends, then ask the worker to take them down
questions.why: Photos of a client's security systems can help thieves and break the client's trust and the company's confidentiality rules. They come down at once; Kevaughn explains why and reports it as the policy on social media says.

questions.q: A small fire starts in a cable tray where the crew is working. Which leadership style fits best at that moment?
o: Supporting: listen to each person's concerns first
Directing: short, clear orders straight away
Delegating: let each worker decide what to do
Coaching: ask questions to help them work it out
questions.why: In an emergency there is no time to consult. The leader gives short, clear, direct orders (raise the alarm, isolate if safe, evacuate, call 110). Consulting styles suit planning and development, not a fire.

questions.q: A visiting engineer from overseas inspects the work while the crew chat in Patois. How should the leading hand speak to the engineer?
o: In Patois, so the engineer gets used to how the crew speaks
Through an apprentice, who can explain the work in simpler terms
As little as possible, and only in writing after the visit is over
In clear standard English, without trade slang he may not know
questions.why: Good communicators adapt to their listener. Patois among the crew is fine, but with clients and visiting engineers the leading hand uses clear standard English and explains or avoids trade slang, so nothing important is misunderstood.

questions.q: In a toolbox talk, a young electrician suggests an idea that will not work on this job. What response keeps ideas coming?
o: Say the idea is poor, so others think before they speak up
Thank him, explain why it won't work here, and ask for more
Ignore it and move straight on to the next point on the list
Agree to use it, so that he does not feel let down in public
questions.why: People stop offering ideas when they are dismissed or ignored. Thanking him, explaining honestly why it does not fit this job, and inviting more keeps the crew thinking; using an idea that will not work wastes time and money.

questions.q: A crew member arrives smelling strongly of alcohol and is unsteady on his feet. What should the leading hand do first?
o: Let him do light tasks on a ladder until he feels better
Joke about it with the crew so he is embarrassed into stopping
Take him off all electrical and height work and keep him safe
Let him drive back to the yard to collect the materials needed
questions.why: An impaired worker is a danger to himself and others. He is taken off electrical work, height work and driving at once, kept safe, and the supervisor is told as the company's policy says. It is handled privately and respectfully, never with jokes.
